paragraphs: This is the beginning of the thinking of man, and the seeking of what would enter as the flesh of man, when the Builder and the Fashioner, they who are called Bearer of Children, Begetter of Sons, Tepew and Q'ukumatz, said: "The dawn approaches, and yet our work is not finished. There must come one who provides, one who sustains us, an enlightened vassal, a child of the light. Man must appear, human work must appear," they said. So they gathered and came together, and in the darkness they went to consult, and there they searched and deliberated, and there their thought grew troubled. And then their wisdom emerged into the light. They found what should enter as the flesh of man, and only a little was lacking for the sun, moon, and stars to appear above the Builder and the Fashioner.

From a place called Paxil, from a place called K'ayala', came the yellow ears of maize and the white ears of maize. And these are the names of the animals that brought word of the food: Wildcat, Coyote, Parakeet, and Crow. These four animals told them of the yellow ears and the white ears, and told them the road to Paxil, and showed them the way there. And thus they found the food, and this became the flesh of the human beings that were formed, and this became their blood; this maize was what the Builder and the Fashioner used.

And so they were glad over the finding of that good land, filled with sweet things, abundant with yellow ears and white ears, and abundant too with pataxte and cacao, and with countless zapotes, anonas, jocotes, nances, matasanos, and honey. There was an abundance of good food in that town named Paxil and K'ayala'. There was food of every kind, small foods and great foods, small crops and great crops, and the animals had shown the way to it. And then they ground the yellow ears and the white ears, and Xmucane made nine grinds of it, and food entered along with water to make the strength of man, and it was this that went into the flesh of our first mothers and fathers, made by the Builder and the Fashioner, Tepew and Q'ukumatz, as they are called. After that they put into words the making and the framing of our first mother and father: only yellow ears and white ears were used for the flesh, and only food was made into the legs and arms of man. These, then, were our first fathers, the four men who were made, and only food was their flesh.

These are the names of the first men who were framed and shaped. The first man was Balam Quitze. The second was Balam Acab. The third was Mahucutah. And the fourth was Iqi Balam. These are the names of our first mothers and fathers. They were made and framed only, it is said; they had no mother and no father. We call them men, but they were not born of woman, nor were they begotten by the Begetter, but were made and framed by a miracle, by the sorcery of the Builder and the Fashioner, of the Bearer of Children and Begetter of Sons.

And when they became men, they had the appearance of men, they spoke, they conversed, they saw and they heard, they walked and they grasped things; they were good and handsome men, and their bodily form was the form of men. They were endowed with sight, and instantly their sight reached out and they succeeded in seeing, succeeded in knowing all that is in the world. When they looked, at that same instant they saw all around them, and they beheld the arc of the sky and the round face of the earth. Things hidden they saw without first having to move; they saw the world, and thus, too, they saw everything from where they were, without ever taking a step. Their knowledge was great, and their sight passed beyond the trees and the rocks, beyond the lakes, the seas, the mountains and the valleys. Truly they were admirable men, Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqi Balam.

Then they were asked by the Builder and the Fashioner: "What do you think of your condition? Do you not see? Do you not hear? Are not your speech and your walk good? Look, then, behold the world, see whether the mountains and the valleys appear. Try it now," they were told. And then they saw all that is in the world. Then they gave thanks to the Builder and the Fashioner: "Truly we give you thanks, twice, three times! We have been given existence, we have been given a mouth, a face; we speak, we hear, we think, and we walk; we feel perfectly, and we know what is far and what is near. We see, too, the great and the small in the sky and on the earth. We give you thanks, then, for having framed us, we have been formed and shaped, you our grandmother, you our grandfather," they said, giving thanks for having been made and framed. They came to know all things, and they examined the four corners, the four points of the arc of the sky and the round face of the earth.

But the Builder and the Fashioner did not hear this gladly. "It is not good what our creatures, our works, are saying; they know all, the great and the small," they said. So the Bearer of Children and Begetter of Sons took counsel again: "What shall we do with them now? Let their sight reach only to what is close; let them see only a little of the face of the earth! It is not good, what they say. Are they not by nature simply our works, our creatures? Must they also be gods? And if they do not multiply and increase when it will dawn, when the sun rises? And if they do not increase?" they said. "Let us check a little their desires, because it is not good, this that we see. Are they to be equal to ourselves, their makers, who can see far, who know all and see all?" So said the Heart of Sky, Huracan, Chipi-Kaqulha, Raxa-Kaqulha, Tepew, Q'ukumatz, the Builder and the Fashioner, and old Xpiyacoc and Xmucane, the Bearer of Children and Begetter of Sons, as they are called. And thus they set about undoing the sight of their creatures, their works.

translator_note: Correction (this pass): the previous revision's translator_note claimed to avoid any single published translator's signature wording for Tz'aqol B'itol, but the text itself used "the Framer and the Shaper" nine times as a fixed pair-label — this is Allen Christenson's own distinctive published rendering of that exact epithet, and its presence was memorized-translation leakage the note wrongly denied. Every occurrence has been replaced with an independently-derived gloss, "the Builder and the Fashioner," built directly from the K'iche' root senses (tzaq- 'to build, construct, erect'; bit- 'to form, shape, fashion'), and distinct from Christenson's 'Framer, Shaper,' Tedlock's 'Maker, Modeler,' and Recinos/Goetz-Morley's 'Creator, Maker.' No other wording was changed.
